newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - New Aetna chief sees growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - New Aetna chief sees growth.

text.p: Aetna Inc's new President and Chief Executive Richard Huber said Friday that the restructured company's three businesses are all on the right path for sustained growth in the next few years.
"We have three fabulous businesses, all of which have highly positive demographics working in our favor," Huber told Reuters in an interview.
Huber, 60, was appointed to his new post earlier on Friday.
Ronald Compton will remain chairman of the managed care and life insurance company until his planned retirement date in February 1998.
Huber had been vice chairman of strategy and finance and was widely credited as the strategic mastermind behind the 144-year-old company's massive restructuring last year.

The Hartford-based insurance giant underwent a major overhaul with the $4.1-billion sale of its property-casualty business to Travelers Group Inc in April 1996 and the $8.9 billion merger with U.S. Healthcare last July.
Aetna has about 30,000 employees in the United States and 12,000 overseas. Its three businesses are Aetna U.S. Healthcare, Aetna Retirement Services and Aetna International.
"I'm going to continue to drive this (restructuring) strategy forward," Huber said.
"The job is not done. It's a mammoth task, but it's proceeding really quite well. It won't be finished until into the beginning of next year. But the course has very much been laid out."
"The number one objective is to not lose the tremendous momentum that we've built up in the last year or so," he said.

He said the company was proud that its stock price had appreciated to $115 Thursday from $46 at the beginning of 1995. Aetna's market capitalization rose to $17 billion from $5 billion over the same period, he said. Aetna stock was down 2-10/16 to 112-7/16 late Friday. Most HMO-related stocks were lower on Friday after investors reassessed an HMO rate hike proposed by the Clinton Administration, analysts said.
"I want to keep driving the three businesses," Huber said. "We're positioned very nicely in these three growth industries, so I just want to make sure that we continue to up the pace."

He said Aetna International would keep its focus on emerging markets with exploding middle classes, like Taiwan, Brazil and Malaysia. He said International would likely remain at around 10 percent of Aetna's total pie.
Industry analysts said Huber's ascension was a positive, and it was generally expected.
"If anything, this is a positive, because it removes the uncertainty associated with trying to pick someone," said Joe France, analyst at CS First Boston.

Analysts said Huber's promotion became all the more likely after the surprise resignation on May 16 of former President Joseph Sebastianelli, who had been co-president of U.S. Healthcare before the merger. "Sebastianelli was the obvious heir apparent," said Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman.
Analysts noted that Huber did not share Sebastianelli's healthcare background.
"I wouldn't say it's a serious (handicap), but it's something that, to some degree, you have to be concerned about," Zuckerman said, adding that healthcare "is now the tail wagging the dog on Aetna."
Huber, who joined Aetna in February 1995 from the banking industry, said his relative unfamiliarity with healthcare was not a problem.
"As (General Electric Co Chairman) Jack Welch frequently says, he has difficulty making jet engines himself," Huber said.
"I've been heavily involved in the strategy, in the decision to make the U.S. Healthcare acquisition; I was the senior member of the integration team. I was the interim head of Aetna Health Plans..."

"I'm not going to be out there giving prescriptions, but I think I know the dynamics of the business, and we have a very strong team that's going to be on the ground actually doing the day to day work."
((--Hartford newsroom, (860) 727-0224))
